C011.subject: The trade-off between meta-rule evolution and system stability
C011.object: the slow-timescale meta-rules impose a hard invariant that prohibits any fast-timescale rule from directly referencing or modifying the system's core reward function
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: The trade-off between meta-rule evolution and system stability the slow-timescale meta-rules impose a hard invariant that prohibits any fast-timescale rule from directly referencing or modifying the system's core reward function]

[PATH:empirical] Conduct a controlled simulation experiment comparing two AGI architectures: one with a hard invariant protecting the core reward function from fast-timescale rules, and one without. Measure stability (e.g., reward variance, convergence time) and meta-rule evolution rate (e.g., number of meta-rule changes over time) across multiple training runs. — Directly tests the hypothesis by creating counterfactual conditions; if the invariant eliminates the trade-off, the architecture with the invariant should show both high stability and unimpeded meta-rule evolution, while the other exhibits the trade-off.

[PATH:literature] Review and meta-analyze existing literature on meta-learning stability in hierarchical reinforcement learning and multi-agent systems, focusing on cases where reward functions are protected (e.g., via hard-coded constraints or constitutional AI approaches) versus open to modification. — Provides an indirect test by synthesizing prior findings; if the hypothesis holds, studies with hard invariants on reward functions should report fewer stability-evolution conflicts than those without, offering empirical support across diverse systems.

[PATH:theoretical] Develop a formal theoretical model of a two-timescale rule system (e.g., using dynamical systems or game theory) to prove whether a hard invariant prohibiting fast-timescale reward modification is necessary and sufficient to eliminate the trade-off, or if other conditions (e.g., invariant strength, rule complexity) matter. — Clarifies the logical necessity and sufficiency of the proposed condition; a rigorous proof could confirm the hypothesis under idealized assumptions, while counterexamples would refute or refine it.
